Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching simplicial mesh as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Set $C_{-1}(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)=0$.
For $0\le k\le d$, let
$C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)$ be the free abelian group generated by ordered
$k$-faces $[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$, with the orientation relation
$$[v_{\pi(0)},\ldots,v_{\pi(k)}]=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$$
for every permutation $\pi$. Define $\partial_0:C_0\to C_{-1}$ to be the
zero map. For $1\le k\le d$, define the **simplicial boundary**
homomorphism $\partial_k:C_k\to C_{k-1}$ on a generator by
$$\partial_k[v_0,\ldots,v_k]:=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j [v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_k].$$
This is the oriented incidence convention; no geometric
integration is part of the definition. The identity
$\partial_{k-1}\partial_k=0$ is proved directly from this alternating
formula in the following lemma.

derivations.claim: If $k=1$, then $\partial_{k-1}=\partial_0=0$ by the definition, so the double boundary vanishes. Now let $k\ge2$ and fix an oriented generator $[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$. In $\partial_{k-1}\partial_k[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$, a codimension-two face is obtained by deleting a unique pair of vertices with indices $i<j$. Deleting $i$ first contributes coefficient $(-1)^i(-1)^{j-1}$ because the original index $j$ shifts down by one; deleting $j$ first contributes $(-1)^j(-1)^i$.

The sum of those two coefficients is $(-1)^{i+j-1}+(-1)^{i+j}=0$. Every codimension-two face arises from exactly these two deletion orders, so every basis coefficient in the double boundary is zero. The double boundary therefore vanishes on each generator and, by linearity, on all of $C_k$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a normed vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

derivations.claim: If $N=0$, then $\widehat P=\{0\}$ and the empty sum defines the unique linear map $X\to\widehat P$; all degree-of-freedom identities are vacuous and reproduction holds for the sole element $p=0$. For $N\ge1$, define $\widehat I v=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i$. The sum is finite and each coefficient is linear in $v$, so $\widehat I$ is a well-defined linear map into $\widehat P$. Applying the $j$th degree of freedom gives $\widehat\sigma_j(\widehat I v)=\sum_i\widehat\sigma_i(v) \widehat\sigma_j(\widehat\phi_i)=\widehat\sigma_j(v)$ by [F1].

If $p\in\widehat P$, then both $p$ and $\widehat I p$ have the same degree-of-freedom vector, by step 1.1; injectivity of $J_{\widehat\Sigma}$ therefore gives $\widehat I p=p$. If another $J:X\to\widehat P$ has the same degree-of-freedom values, then $J_{\widehat\Sigma}(Jv-\widehat I v)=0$, and injectivity again gives $Jv=\widehat I v$. This proves uniqueness.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Then any two norms on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are
equivalent ([[def-equivalent-norms]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

More precisely, for every norm $N$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ there are reals
$c > 0$ and $C' > 0$ with

$$c\,\lVert x\rVert_2 \;\le\; N(x) \;\le\; C'\,\lVert x\rVert_2 \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathbb{R}^{n},$$

and the general statement follows because equivalence of norms is an equivalence
relation.

**Consequently all the metric notions on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are norm independent**
for $n \ge 1$: any two norms give the same open sets, the same convergent
sequences with the same limits, the same Cauchy sequences and the same uniformly
continuous maps ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is used twice in the proof and both uses are marked**:
once so that the constant $C$ of
[[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] exists, and once
so that the Euclidean unit sphere is **nonempty**, which is what the extreme
value theorem needs. At $n = 0$ the conclusion is true but vacuous, the zero
space carrying exactly one norm ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and it is not
obtained from the argument below.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $M$
and $N$ be norms on $V$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). $M$ and $N$ are
**equivalent** when there are reals $c > 0$ and $C > 0$ with

$$c\,M(v) \;\le\; N(v) \;\le\; C\,M(v) \qquad \text{for every } v \in V .$$

The constants are not part of the data and are not unique: any smaller $c$ and
any larger $C$ serve as well.

### This is an equivalence relation on the norms on $V$

- **Reflexive:** take $c = C = 1$.
- **Symmetric:** from $cM \le N \le CM$ and $c, C > 0$ one gets
  $C^{-1}N \le M \le c^{-1}N$, dividing by the positive constants
  ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).
- **Transitive:** if $cM \le N \le CM$ and $c'N \le P \le C'N$ then
  $c'c\,M \le P \le C'C\,M$, and $c'c > 0$, $C'C > 0$, a product of positives
  being positive.

### The dictionary with equivalent metrics

Let $d_M(u,v) = M(u-v)$ and $d_N(u,v) = N(u-v)$ be the induced metrics
([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Substituting $v := u - w$ in the displayed
condition gives

$$c\,d_M(u,w) \;\le\; d_N(u,w) \;\le\; C\,d_M(u,w) \qquad \text{for all } u, w \in V ,$$

which is **verbatim the Lipschitz equivalence** of $d_M$ and $d_N$ in the sense
of [[def-equivalent-metrics]], with $\alpha = c$ and $\beta = C$. That is the
**strongest** of the three tiers that item distinguishes: by
[[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]], Lipschitz equivalence implies uniform
equivalence, which implies topological equivalence. So equivalent norms give

- the same open sets, hence the same closed sets, closures and interiors
  ([[def-metric-topology]]);
- the same uniformly continuous maps into and out of $V$
  ([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]);
- the same convergent sequences with the same limits, and the same Cauchy
  sequences ([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]]).

The last line deserves its two-line verification, since it is used constantly
below and is not literally a clause of [[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]]. If
$d_M(v_k, v) \to 0$ then $0 \le d_N(v_k,v) \le C\,d_M(v_k,v)$, so given a
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ an index beyond which $d_M(v_k,v) < \varepsilon/C$
serves for $d_N$; the converse uses $d_M \le c^{-1}d_N$ in the same way. The
Cauchy statement is the same estimate applied to $d_N(v_k,v_l)$. In particular
$(V, d_M)$ is complete if and only if $(V,d_N)$ is.

**Naming.** Many texts say *strongly equivalent* for what
[[def-equivalent-metrics]] calls Lipschitz equivalent, and simply *equivalent*
for what it calls topologically equivalent. As there, this library always writes
the qualifier for metrics. For **norms** there is no fork to guard against: the
condition displayed above is the only one anyone calls equivalence of norms, and
it is always the Lipschitz-strength one.

Let $X$ be a complex vector space carrying two complex norms $\|\cdot\|_a$ and
$\|\cdot\|_b$, and suppose $X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then
$\|\cdot\|_a$ and $\|\cdot\|_b$ are equivalent in the sense of
[[def-equivalent-complex-norms]].

Let $M$ and $N$ be complex norms ([[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]) on the same complex vector space $V$. They are **equivalent complex norms** if there are positive real constants $c,C\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$
cM(v)\le N(v)\le CM(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.
$$
Both inequalities and the positivity of $c,C$ are in the real complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], with completeness established in [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]); the vector scalar field remains $\mathbb C$. No order comparison of complex numbers is intended.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

If it is zero, then for finite $q$ the continuous polynomial vanishes almost everywhere, and for $q=\infty$ it vanishes essentially everywhere. In either case, if it were nonzero at an interior point, continuity would make it bounded away from zero on an interior ball of positive measure, a contradiction. It therefore vanishes on the open simplex and hence is the zero polynomial, since its finite Taylor expansion at any interior point is exact.

If $\widehat P=\{0\}$, all displayed estimates and functional bounds hold immediately, so assume $\dim\widehat P>0$. The expression $N_1(v):=\|v\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)}+|v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat S_d)} +\|v\|_{L^p(\widehat F)}$ is a norm: it is nonnegative, homogeneous and subadditive, and $N_1(v)=0$ forces the cell $L^p$ norm to vanish, so the preceding argument gives $v=0$. In either case, norm equivalence gives $N_1(v)\le C N_0(v)$. Taking the maximum over the finitely many facets proves their uniform estimate. By [F3], any degree-of-freedom functional is linear on $\widehat P$; it is bounded for $N_1$ by finite-dimensional norm equivalence and hence by $N_0$.

If $\widehat P=\{0\}$, the second estimate is immediate. If $m=0$, the second estimate is the derivative part of step 2.1 with its order there set to $\ell$. Otherwise add the target seminorm $|v|_{W^{\ell,p}}$ to the quotient norm; it is well-defined because it also vanishes on $\widehat P\cap\mathbb P_{m-1}$. The sum is another norm. Applying [F1] or [F2] to these two norms bounds the target seminorm by the order-$m$ seminorm. This proves the second estimate.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $a$ be the barycenter of $\widehat S_d$ and, for $0<t<1$, set $F_t(x)=a+t(x-a)$. The set $S_t:=F_t^{-1}(\widehat S_d)$ is open and contains $\overline{\widehat S_d}$: each point of the closure is carried to a strict convex combination of that point and the interior point $a$, which lies in the open simplex. Thus $u_t:=u\circ F_t$ is defined on $S_t$ for $u\in W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)$, and [F1] gives $D^\alpha u_t=t^{|\alpha|}(D^\alpha u)\circ F_t$.

For every $g\in L^p(\widehat S_d)$, $g\circ F_t\to g$ in $L^p(\widehat S_d)$ as $t\uparrow1$. To see this, extend $g$ by zero to $\mathbb R^d$ and approximate that extension in $L^p$ by $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ using [F2]. For $t\ge1/2$, change of variables bounds the pullback error by $t^{-d/p}\|g-\phi\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}\le2^{d/p}\|g-\phi\|_p$; for fixed $\phi$, uniform continuity on the compact closure gives $\phi\circ F_t\to\phi$ uniformly there. First choosing $\phi$ with arbitrarily small error and then taking $t\uparrow1$ proves the claim. Applying it to each of the finitely many $D^\alpha u$ and using [F1] shows $u_t|_{\widehat S_d}\to u$ in $W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)$.

Fix $t<1$. Since $\overline{\widehat S_d}$ is compactly contained in $S_t$, choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(S_t)$ equal to one near that closure by [F3]. Then $\eta u_t\in W^{k,p}(S_t)$ has compact support in $S_t$, so its zero extension $U_t$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ by [F3]. By [F2], choose $\phi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ converging to $U_t$ in that norm. Since $U_t=u_t$ on a neighbourhood of the closed simplex, the restrictions $\phi_j|_{\widehat S_d}$ converge to $u_t|_{\widehat S_d}$ in $W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)$.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $t$ close enough to one that $\|u_t-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)}<\varepsilon/2$ by step 2.1, and then choose $j$ in step 2.2 with $\|\phi_j-u_t\|_{W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)}<\varepsilon/2$. The triangle inequality gives $\|\phi_j-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)}<\varepsilon$. The choices are finite for each $u,\varepsilon$; Countable Choice is only the declared background of [F4], and no $p=\infty$ density is used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $z\in\overline{\widehat S_d}$. Define the barycentric affine coordinates by $\lambda_0(x)=1-\sum_{i=1}^dx_i$ and $\lambda_i(x)=x_i$ for $1\le i\le d$; they sum to one and are nonnegative exactly on the closed simplex. The active set $I(z)=\{i:\lambda_i(z)=0\}$ has at most $d$ elements, and the gradients of the corresponding coordinates are linearly independent. Complete these affine coordinates to an invertible affine coordinate system $y=(\lambda_i)_{i\in I(z)},y_{m+1},\ldots,y_d$, where $m=|I(z)|$. Because every inactive barycentric coordinate is strictly positive at $z$, a sufficiently small neighbourhood $U_z$ meets the simplex exactly in the orthant chart $y_1>0,\ldots,y_m>0$; for $m=0$ it is an interior chart.

The charts $U_z$ cover the compact closure, so [F4] gives a finite subcover. Shrink them to open sets $V_j$ still covering the closure, with $\overline V_j\subset U_j$. Use [F3] to choose smooth cutoffs $\theta_j$ supported compactly in $U_j$ and equal to one on $V_j$. Their sum $S$ is positive on a neighbourhood $N$ of the closed simplex. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported compactly in $N$ and equal to one near the closed simplex, and set $\eta_j=\chi\theta_j/S$ on $N$, zero outside $N$. Then each $\eta_j$ is smooth and supported in its chart, and their sum is one near the simplex. Each localized input $\eta_j u$ has norm bounded by a fixed multiple of $\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)}$ by the product rule in [F3].

In an interior chart, the localized function is zero near the chart edge. Its zero extension to $\mathbb R^d$ has the same weak derivatives: for any test function, multiply that test by a cutoff equal to one on the localized support, apply the weak identity on the chart, and note that all derivatives of the cutoff product agree on that support. This is the zero-extension part of [F3]. In a boundary chart with $m$ active faces, the localized function is a $W^{k,p}$ function on the orthant $O_m=(0,\infty)^m\times\mathbb R^{d-m}$ and vanishes near the artificial edge of the chart; extend by zero across only that artificial edge using the same test-function argument.

Extend from $O_m$ to $\mathbb R^d$ one coordinate at a time. At each stage, apply the reflected half-space formula in [F2] to the coordinate being extended, with the other $m-1$ positive coordinates as tangential variables. For clarity, the coordinate formula on $t<0$ is $\sum_{j=1}^k a_jw(x',-jt)$, with $\sum_ja_j(-j)^r=1$ for $0\le r<k$; for $k=0$ use even reflection. For a test compactly supported in $O_{m-1}\times\mathbb R$, apply the half-space proof's normal ACL trace and integration-by-parts identity on each compact tangential subdomain and then exhaust the test support by finitely many such subdomains. Tangential weak derivatives pass through the finite reflection sum by the weak test identity, and the displayed moment equations cancel every normal interface term. The change of variable $s=-jt$ bounds each reflected derivative in $L^p$ by the same finite coefficient sum as in [F2] (and by the corresponding essential supremum sum at $p=\infty$). Thus this explicit operator is bounded on $W^{k,p}(O_m)$ and extends one orthant coordinate. Repeating at most $m\le d$ times gives the required extension. Pulling back through the affine chart changes the bound by a finite factor from [F1].

Apply these local bounded linear extensions to the finitely many localized pieces and add them. Their sum is bounded and linear, and on $\widehat S_d$ its restriction is $\sum_j\eta_j u=u$. There are finitely many charts, all have bounded coordinate images and the reflection operators add support only by fixed finite factors, so the sum is supported in a fixed bounded set. The definition of extension domain in [F3] gives the conclusion.

$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $v=0$ and the conclusion is immediate. Assume henceforth $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. Extend $v$ by zero to $\widetilde v$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and define $g_i$ to be its cellwise derivative on mesh cells and zero outside $\overline\Omega$. On each cell apply the simplex Green formula to $v\varphi e_i$ for an arbitrary $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. Fact [F1] gives the cell identity. Interior facet terms cancel by [F2]; boundary facet terms vanish by the zero-boundary clause of [F2]. Summing the finitely many cell identities gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\widetilde v\,\partial_i\varphi =-\int_{\mathbb R^d}g_i\varphi.$$ Both functions are in $L^p$, so [F7] gives $\widetilde v\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ with gradient $g$.

Put $d_\Omega(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$, which is $1$-Lipschitz. Choose a smooth scalar step $\theta$ with $\theta(s)=0$ for $s\le1$, $\theta(s)=1$ for $s\ge2$, and $0\le\theta\le1$. For $\epsilon>0$ set $\zeta_\epsilon(x)=\theta(d_\Omega(x)/\epsilon)$ and convolve it with a nonnegative smooth mollifier of integral one supported in the ball of radius $\epsilon/4$, obtaining $\eta_\epsilon$. Then $\eta_\epsilon$ is smooth, supported in $\Omega$, equals zero where $d_\Omega\le3\epsilon/4$, equals one where $d_\Omega\ge9\epsilon/4$, and $\|\nabla\eta_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|\theta'\|_\infty/\epsilon$. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, its support is compact in $\Omega$.

Let $M$ be the maximum of the cellwise suprema of $|\nabla v|$. Across every interior facet the polynomial traces agree; on every boundary facet they agree with zero. For a point $x$ in the mesh skeleton, its minimal mesh face is the unique mesh face whose relative interior contains $x$; the local star of that face means the union of the cells containing it. If the minimal face is a facet, there are exactly two incident cells at an interior facet and exactly one at a boundary facet. In the interior case their values at $x$ agree by the matching polynomial traces; in the boundary case the single cell value agrees with exterior zero by the zero boundary trace. For the remaining faces, let $c\ge2$ be their codimension. The incident simplicial cones in their local star cut a small sphere in the normal space of the face, of dimension $c-1$, into a finite face-to-face triangulation of the local directions in $\Omega$. Within each connected component, top-dimensional pieces are connected by facet adjacency: perturb a path in that open component to avoid the finite union of codimension-two faces. At an interior point the direction set is the whole sphere, which is connected because $c\ge2$, so matching traces make all incident polynomial values agree. At a boundary point every component has a boundary direction; following facet adjacencies reaches a boundary facet, where the polynomial value is zero, so all cell limits in that component are zero. Thus in all cases the cellwise continuous representatives and the exterior zero fit continuously on the whole finite polyhedral partition. Restrict this continuous function to any line segment. The segment is divided by the finitely many cell facets into finitely many intervals; on each cell interval its derivative along the segment has magnitude at most $M$, and on exterior intervals it is zero. Continuity at the interval endpoints then gives $|\widetilde v(x)-\widetilde v(y)|\le M|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Thus $|v(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$.

The difference $v-\eta_\epsilon v$ and its weak gradient are supported in $E_\epsilon=\{x\in\Omega:d_\Omega(x)<9\epsilon/4\}$. On this layer, step 2.1 gives $|v|\le(9/4)M\epsilon$, and step 1.2 gives $|v\nabla\eta_\epsilon|\le(9/4)M\|\theta'\|_\infty$. Also $|\nabla v|\le M$. The sets $E_{1/n}$ decrease to the empty set and $|E_1|\le|\Omega|<\infty$, so [F5] gives $|E_{1/n}|\to0$. These bounds show $\|v-\eta_{1/n}v\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\to0$ for finite $p$.

Each $\eta_{1/n}v$ has compact support in $\Omega$. By [F5] extend it by zero to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ and approximate there by $\phi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one near the compact support of $\eta_{1/n}v$. Then $\chi\phi_j\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and, by the weak product rule, $\chi\phi_j\to\eta_{1/n}v$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$. A diagonal choice with step 3.1 proves $v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ by [F3].
A bounded set is bounded in some direction, so apply [F4] to the membership just proved. Its slab width is finite and gives the displayed Poincare inequality.

derivations.claim: First take $u$ smooth. For $x,y\in\widehat S_d$, convexity keeps $z_t=tx+(1-t)y$ in the simplex. The segment identity and $|x-y|\le h:=\operatorname{diam}(\widehat S_d)$ give $$|u(x)-u(y)|^p\le h^p\int_0^1|\nabla u(tx+(1-t)y)|^p\,dt,$$ by [F2] and Jensen on the unit interval. Jensen again gives $$|u(x)-u_{\widehat S_d}|^p\le|\widehat S_d|^{-1} \int_{\widehat S_d}|u(x)-u(y)|^p\,dy.$$

Integrate the last bound over $x$. For $t\ge1/2$, fix $y$ and use $x\mapsto tx+(1-t)y$; its Jacobian is $t^d$, and its image is contained in the simplex, so its integral is at most $2^d\int_{\widehat S_d}|\nabla u|^p$. For $t\le1/2$, fix $x$ and use $y\mapsto tx+(1-t)y$, whose inverse Jacobian is at most $2^d$, giving the same bound. Tonelli [F3] therefore yields $$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_p^p\le2^dh^p\|\nabla u\|_p^p.$$ Taking $p$th roots proves the estimate for smooth $u$.

For arbitrary $u\in W^{1,p}$ choose smooth $u_j\to u$ in $W^{1,p}$ by [F1]. Holder on the finite-measure simplex gives $\int u_j\to\int u$, so $(u_j)_{\widehat S_d}\to u_{\widehat S_d}$; also $\|u_j-u\|_p\to0$ and $\|\nabla u_j\|_p\to\|\nabla u\|_p$. Passing to the limit in the smooth inequality of step 2.1 proves the statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: The monomials $x^\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le r-1$ form a basis of $\mathbb P_{r-1}$. Thus if $N$ is the number of these multi-indices, then $N=\dim\mathbb P_{r-1}$. Define the linear moment map $M:\mathbb P_{r-1}\to\mathbb R^N$ by $M(q)_\alpha=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q$. If every component is zero, take the largest degree $m$ of a nonzero homogeneous part of $q$. For each $|\alpha|=m$, $D^\alpha q$ is the constant $\alpha!$ times the coefficient of $x^\alpha$ in that highest homogeneous part; its zero mean forces that coefficient to vanish. This contradicts the choice of $m$. Repeating downward shows $q=0$, so $M$ is injective and, since its domain and codomain have the same finite dimension, bijective.

The vector of means of $D^\alpha v$, $|\alpha|\le r-1$, is defined because each derivative is in $L^p$ on the finite-measure simplex and therefore in $L^1$ by [F4]. By bijectivity in step 1.1 there is a unique $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}$ with those moments. For $w=v-q$, each derivative $D^\alpha w$, $|\alpha|\le r-1$, has zero mean; and every derivative of $q$ of order at least $r$ is zero.

Apply [F1] to every mean-zero derivative of order $r-1$ in step 2.1; its $L^p$ norm is bounded by the $L^p$ norms of derivatives of order $r$ of $v$, since $D^r q=0$. Apply [F1] successively to derivatives of orders $r-2,r-3,\ldots,0$, each of which also has zero mean; at each stage its norm is bounded by the next derivative order already controlled. Thus all derivatives of $w$ of order at most $r$ are bounded by $C|v|_{W^{r,p}}$. If $s\le r$, retaining only orders through $s$ proves the first clause.

If $s>r$, the same argument controls all derivative orders at most $r-1$ by $C|v|_{W^{r,p}}$. For each $r\le|\beta|\le s$, $D^\beta w=D^\beta v$ because $D^\beta q=0$. Adding the finitely many derivative bounds through order $s$ gives $\|w\|_{W^{s,p}}\le C\sum_{j=r}^s|v|_{W^{j,p}}$, proving the second clause.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a normed vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Let $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
with $N=\dim\widehat P$, dual shape functions $\widehat\phi_i$, and bounded
extensions of its degrees of freedom to a normed function space $X$ containing
$\widehat P$. Then the operator
$$\widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i$$
is the unique linear map $X\to\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat I v)=\widehat\sigma_i(v)$ for every $i$, and
$\widehat I p=p$ for every $p\in\widehat P$.

This is the distributional divergence identity.

For smooth $\widehat v$, differentiate $v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$ componentwise. In three dimensions, write $C=A^{-1}$. For any $z\in\mathbb R^3$ and indices $m,\ell$, the scalar triple product gives $$z\cdot((C^Te_m)\times(C^Te_\ell)) =\det[z,C^Te_m,C^Te_\ell] =\det(C)\det[C^{-T}z,e_m,e_\ell] =\det(C)\,z\cdot(C^{-1}(e_m\times e_\ell)).$$ Since this holds for every $z$, comparing components yields $\epsilon_{ijk}C_{mj}C_{\ell k}=(\det A)^{-1}A_{ir}\epsilon_{rm\ell}$. The chain rule then gives $\operatorname{curl}_xv=(\det A)^{-1}A(\operatorname{curl}_{\widehat x}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$. In two dimensions write $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Delta=ad-bc>0$. Then $v_1=(d\widehat v_1-c\widehat v_2)/\Delta$, $v_2=(-b\widehat v_1+a\widehat v_2)/\Delta$, $\partial_{x_1}=(d\partial_{\widehat x_1}-c\partial_{\widehat x_2})/\Delta$, and $\partial_{x_2}=(-b\partial_{\widehat x_1}+a\partial_{\widehat x_2})/\Delta$. Substituting these four expressions and cancelling the two mixed terms gives $\partial_{x_1}v_2-\partial_{x_2}v_1 =(\det A)^{-1}(\partial_{\widehat x_1}\widehat v_2- \partial_{\widehat x_2}\widehat v_1)\circ F^{-1}$.

The physical field and candidate divergence in step 1.1 lie in $L^2(K)$: affine change of variables makes their squared norms finite constant multiples of the reference squared norms, and multiplication by the fixed matrix $A/(\det A)$ preserves finiteness. For $d=3$, take $\psi\in C_c^\infty(K;\mathbb R^3)$ and set $\widehat\psi=A^T(\psi\circ F)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$. For every integer $k\ge0$ and
$1\le p\le\infty$, there is a bounded linear operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$$
whose restriction to $\widehat S_d$ is the input class. Consequently
$\widehat S_d$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension domain in the sense of
[[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. The operator may
be chosen with support in one fixed bounded set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying

invariance under null-set changes follow from

axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an

linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$

is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$

zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a normed vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>0$ with $\overline{B(c,R)}\subset\widehat S_2$, and choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(c,R))$ equal to one on $B(c,R/2)$. For $0<\epsilon<R/4$, put $L_\epsilon=\log(R/\epsilon)$ and $$u_\epsilon(x)=\chi(x)\, \frac{\log\!\left(R/\sqrt{|x-c|^2+\epsilon^2}\right)}{L_\epsilon}.$$ This is smooth and compactly supported in the simplex, and $u_\epsilon(c)=1$.

In polar coordinates about $c$, $r\ge0$ and the stated range $0<\epsilon<R/4$ gives $r^2+\epsilon^2\ge\epsilon^2>0$ and the radial derivative has no zero denominator. The undivided logarithm has uniformly bounded squared $L^2$ integral on $B(c,R)$: its absolute value is bounded by $\log(R/r)+C$ for $0<r<R$ and small $\epsilon$, and $\int_0^R r(\log(R/r)+C)^2dr<\infty$. Its radial derivative has magnitude $r/(r^2+\epsilon^2)$, so $$\int_0^R\frac{r^3}{(r^2+\epsilon^2)^2}\,dr \le C+\log(R/\epsilon)=C+L_\epsilon,$$ by splitting at $r=\epsilon$. After division by $L_\epsilon$, these estimates show the $L^2$ norm and the gradient contribution from $\chi\nabla\log(R/\sqrt{r^2+\epsilon^2})$ tend to zero. The term $\nabla\chi$ is supported where $R/2\le r<R$, on which the logarithm is uniformly bounded; its divided $L^2$ norm also tends to zero. Therefore $\|u_\epsilon\|_{W^{1,2}(\widehat S_2)}\to0$.

If point evaluation at $c$ were bounded, some finite $C$ would satisfy $|u(c)|\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}$ for every smooth $u$. By [F2] this is the boundedness condition for the candidate nodal functional. Applying it to $u_\epsilon$ gives $1\le C\|u_\epsilon\|_{W^{1,2}}\to0$, a contradiction. Hence evaluation is unbounded at the critical exponent.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching simplicial mesh as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Set $C_{-1}(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)=0$.
For $0\le k\le d$, let
$C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb Z)$ be the free abelian group generated by ordered
$k$-faces $[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$, with the orientation relation
$$[v_{\pi(0)},\ldots,v_{\pi(k)}]=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)[v_0,\ldots,v_k]$$
for every permutation $\pi$. Define $\partial_0:C_0\to C_{-1}$ to be the
zero map. For $1\le k\le d$, define the **simplicial boundary**
homomorphism $\partial_k:C_k\to C_{k-1}$ on a generator by
$$\partial_k[v_0,\ldots,v_k]:=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j [v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_k].$$
This is the oriented incidence convention; no geometric
integration is part of the definition. The identity
$\partial_{k-1}\partial_k=0$ is proved directly from this alternating
formula in the following lemma.

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the first triangle and the ordered triangle $[v_0,v_2,v_3]$ to obtain $$\partial[v_0,v_1,v_2]=[v_1,v_2]-[v_0,v_2]+[v_0,v_1],$$ $$\partial[v_0,v_2,v_3]=[v_2,v_3]-[v_0,v_3]+[v_0,v_2].$$ The edge $[v_0,v_2]$ appears with coefficient $-1$ in the first boundary and $+1$ in the second.

Adding the two formulas cancels the shared diagonal and leaves $[v_0,v_1]+[v_1,v_2]+[v_2,v_3]-[v_0,v_3]$, which is the oriented outer boundary since $-[v_0,v_3]=[v_3,v_0]$. This explicit calculation agrees with the general cancellation rule [F2].
